resources.string: A way into the Tor network when the network itself is blocked. Pick a built-in bridge, fetch what works where you are, or ask for one of your own.
This build does not include the Tor core, so bridges have nothing to configure. Build it with scripts/build-overlay-cores.sh tor.
Your current chain does not use Tor, so these bridges are saved but not used yet. Pick a Tor mode on the Chain page to put them to work.
Tor connects straight to the public relays. Fastest, and the right answer unless your network blocks Tor.
The public list Tor Browser ships. Always available, and blocked first, because everyone has it.
Addresses the Tor Project hands to this device alone. In no public list, but you need a working path to the bridge server to get them.
Lines you already have, from email, from Telegram, or from someone you trust. Only as good as where they came from.
Start with obfs4. Move to Snowflake or WebTunnel when a network blocks fixed addresses rather than the traffic itself.
This build does not include these transports: %1$s. Build them with scripts/build-pt-transports.sh.
Not available: this build has no %1$s binary.
Makes the traffic look like random data. The common choice, the cheapest one, and what most bridges run.
Hops through short-lived volunteer proxies over WebRTC. Good when fixed bridge addresses are blocked; the speed comes and goes.
Looks like an ordinary visit to an HTTPS website. For networks that block anything they cannot recognise.
Hides the connection behind a large CDN. Slow and heavy on data, and the hardest of these to block.
An address and nothing else: no disguise. The only type that needs no extra binary, so it works in every build.
These are public, and everybody uses the same ones, so a censor can have them on a list. When they stop working, ask for a personal bridge instead.
No built-in bridge of this type. Refresh the list, or request a personal one.

The request goes to bridges.torproject.org through your live tunnel when one is up, and directly when it is not. On a network that blocks Tor that address is usually blocked too, so connect with Aether or Psiphon first, then come back and fetch.
Two letters. Leave it empty to let the server guess from your address, which with a tunnel up is the country of the tunnel exit rather than yours.
Never refreshed on this device: the list that ships with the app is in use.
One request returns two or three addresses that are in no public list. The pool is rate-limited per network, so keep whatever you are given.
The Tor Project does not hand out plain bridges this way. Choose an obfuscated type above.
One bridge per line, exactly as you received it. Other ways to get bridges: send an empty email to bridges@torproject.org from a Gmail or Riseup address, or message @GetBridgesBot on Telegram.
Nothing selected, so Tor will connect the usual way. Tick a bridge above.
%1$d of these needs a transport this build does not have, and will be ignored.
Do not publish a personal bridge. A bridge in a screenshot is a bridge that gets reported and blocked, for you and for whoever else was given it.
The Tor Project reports that no bridge is needed in %1$s: plain Tor should connect.
Could not reach bridges.torproject.org. Connect with Aether or Psiphon first, then request again.
That captcha answer was refused. Request another one.
No bridge of a type this build supports is available for that country. Try Snowflake, or leave the country empty.
The bridge server refused the request (%1$d). Try again later.
Something answered, but not the bridge server. Your network is rewriting the connection.
Type the characters in the image.
The captcha image could not be shown. Send the request anyway.
Since the Tor Project retired BridgeDB in 2024 this captcha is a static image and the answer is not checked. The app still follows the documented flow, so it keeps working if that ever changes.
If Tor cannot connect at all on your network, the Tor bridges page gives it another way in.
